content: To effectively manage and monitor congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases, it is essential to identify the healthcare facilities where infants with CRS are most likely to be evaluated and treated. These facilities include those specializing in the management of common CRS-related defects, such as cataracts, heart defects, and hearing impairments, as well as centers that care for infants born to mothers with a history of rubella infection during pregnancy. Secondary and tertiary care facilities are the most appropriate locations for CRS surveillance, as they are equipped to handle the evaluation and treatment of these conditions. Including primary healthcare providers in the CRS surveillance system is not necessary and may overwhelm general healthcare providers with additional responsibilities, such as identifying, reporting, and following up on CRS cases. Examples of suitable facilities for CRS surveillance include children’s hospitals, centers for hearing and blindness, and obstetric clinics that manage pregnant women with rubella. If the selected facilities capture the majority of suspected CRS cases in a country, the surveillance system can be considered adequate. Feedback from these pilot sites can then be used to refine the protocols. Local surveillance coordinators at sentinel sites play a critical role in ensuring adherence to national protocols and SOPs for CRS surveillance. Their responsibilities include training healthcare workers, collecting clinical and epidemiological data, completing case investigation forms, ensuring proper specimen collection and transportation, maintaining a line listing of suspected CRS cases, providing feedback to healthcare workers, and maintaining communication with the national coordinator regarding case identification and follow-up. Initial and refresher training sessions for healthcare providers participating in CRS surveillance should be conducted annually. CRS surveillance activities should begin once coordinators and participating sites have been identified and providers have been trained in the relevant SOPs. Surveillance quality assessments should be conducted at sentinel sites at least every six months to evaluate the completeness of CRS case reporting. This involves reviewing hospital records to identify missed cases and assessing the proportion of reported cases that have not undergone laboratory testing. Surveillance data should also be monitored for completeness, and any gaps should be addressed with the healthcare providers involved. In countries where pilot testing has shown that the majority of infants are not included in CRS surveillance, the system should be expanded to include additional sites. The ultimate goal is to establish a sentinel surveillance system that captures the majority of CRS cases nationwide. Feedback on the epidemiology of CRS should be provided to stakeholders, along with recommendations for system improvements. Rubella seroprevalence surveys can complement surveillance activities by providing reliable data on population immunity. For example, a serosurvey in Kyrgyzstan revealed high susceptibility to rubella among women over 25 years of age, leading to targeted vaccination recommendations. Serosurveys can also identify susceptibility among specific cohorts, such as vaccine refusers or populations with limited healthcare access, and guide vaccination strategies to achieve disease control and elimination. Rubella outbreak investigations involve confirming diagnoses through laboratory testing, determining if an outbreak is occurring, establishing a response team, and enhancing surveillance to increase case detection. Active surveillance includes laboratory confirmation of cases, alerting healthcare workers about the outbreak, and establishing a pregnancy registry to document outcomes such as CRS cases and fetal deaths. Supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) are critical for reaching unvaccinated populations and should be planned with detailed microplans that account for local health infrastructure and population density. SIAs should target all children in the specified age group, regardless of vaccination history, and address barriers to reaching underserved populations. In summary, a robust CRS surveillance and vaccination strategy, supported by serosurveys and SIAs, is essential for controlling and eliminating rubella and preventing the devastating consequences of CRS.
